--- type: framework source_url: "https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack" runs_on: [] sources: "Lauren Tan (poteto) — pstack v0.15.2, cursor/plugins (github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack), MIT (2026); README.md, plugin.json, poteto-mode SKILL.md, 48 skill/agent frontmatters, benny automation pack" raw: ["../../raw/pstack/2026-09-11-pstack-plugin.md"] updated: 2026-09-11 --- # pstack **Workflow** — the primary skill per [SDLC stage](../sdlc-stage/index.md) this framework runs. Note how much of it is off-spine: pstack ships no specify stage at all, and its planning capability is an escape hatch rather than a step. ```mermaid flowchart TB A["pstack-how · pstack-why
Align"] --> P["pstack-architect
pstack-figure-it-out
Plan"] --> I["pstack-tdd · pstack-recall
Implement"] I --> V["pstack-create-verification-skill
Validate"] I --> R["pstack-interrogate
pstack-blast-radius · pstack-no-comments
Review"] V --> L["pstack-reflect · pstack-teach
Learn"] R --> L M(["pstack-poteto-mode
23 playbooks · 23 principles"]) -.routes.-> A M -.routes.-> P M -.routes.-> I M -.routes.-> V M -.routes.-> R ``` **pstack** is Lauren Tan's (poteto — React core team, previously Meta and Netflix, currently Cursor) MIT-licensed **Cursor plugin**: 25 skills, 23 principle skills, 2 subagents, 23 playbooks, and a dormant automation pack. Its thesis is stated against the grain of the whole category: > "there's a growing sense that ai writes too much slop code. i agree. i don't want to ship like a team of twenty slop artists. **throughput without quality is not a goal i aspire to. if you want to go fast, go deep first.** […] the goal is not to maximize loc, in fact it's the opposite. pstack helps you write less, but higher quality code." The argument connecting depth to speed is the framework's actual claim: **"pstack gives you fearless parallelism. when you can go deep on one agent and trust it to write good, verifiable code, you can truly parallelize with confidence."** Rigor is not a tax on throughput here, it is the precondition for it — you can only run many agents at once if you trust each one's output without reading it. Two steps constitute the entire getting-started instruction: run [[pstack-setup-pstack]] to pick models per role, then use [[pstack-poteto-mode]] whenever the work needs rigor. Everything else is situational and the mode routes to it. - **Root router:** [[pstack-poteto-mode]] — a **sticky mode** that matches the task to one of 23 playbooks, copies its steps into a todo list verbatim, and routes to the other skills as the steps fire. - **Its subagent twin:** [[pstack-poteto-agent]] — the same wrapper as a delegate, because a generic subagent starts without the mode loaded and drifts. - **Install:** `/add-plugin pstack`. It is one of the plugins in Cursor's own `cursor/plugins` marketplace repository. ## Distinctive contributions to the ontology - **The first framework here that is not Cursor-portable but Cursor-*native*.** Every other framework in this wiki is documented as running across many harnesses — [[superpowers]] on six, [[gstack]] on ten, [[speckit]] on thirty. pstack is a **Cursor plugin** and is built on Cursor-specific machinery throughout: plugin-manifest skill and agent roots, `mode: true` sticky skills with a re-injected `reminder` field, `paths:`-attached skills, `~/.cursor/rules/*.mdc` always-applied rules, `Task` subagents with per-call `model` / `readonly` / `environment: cloud` / `cloud_base_branch`, webhook routines, and `~/.cursor/projects/*/agent-transcripts/` as a mineable corpus. **The `runs_on:` edge is deliberately empty** because Cursor has no `harness` page yet — see [Harness gap](#harness-gap-cursor) below. - **Principles as a first-class, citable layer.** 23 one-rule skills, indexed inline by the mode skill and grouped Core / Architecture / Verification / Delegation / Meta. The index is read at task start; a leaf is read in full only when its principle is applied. The non-negotiable that makes the layer real: **name each principle that shaped a decision and the specific choice it changed, and cite only principles whose leaf you read this session.** No other framework here carries an explicitly-cited rule set of this size — the nearest relative is [[speckit]]'s [[pattern-project-constitution]], which is one document rather than a navigable, individually-loadable corpus. - **Model diversity in place of persona diversity.** [[pstack-interrogate]] says it outright: *"the adversarial signal comes from model diversity, not assigned personas."* Every reviewer gets the identical prompt and rubric and differs only in which model runs it. That is a direct rejection of the [[pattern-parallel-persona-review]] approach [[gstack]], [[bmad]], and [[addy-agent-skills]] take, and it makes pstack the wiki's purest [[pattern-cross-model-review]] instance. **The framework is multi-model by construction**, not as an option: [[pstack-setup-pstack]] exists solely to map roles to models, and [[pstack-how]], [[pstack-arena]], [[pstack-architect]], [[pstack-reflect]], and [[pstack-swarm]] each split work across model strengths. - **It refuses to plan, and says why.** *"why are there no planning skills? cursor already has a great plan mode which works great with pstack. but personally, i don't believe in planning. **the best spec is code.**"* There is no specify stage here at all and no spec artifact — the sharpest possible contrast with the spec-driven pole ([[speckit]], [[openspec]], [[nano-spec]], [[agent-os]]). What planning exists is [[pstack-figure-it-out]], reached only when **no** playbook fits, and [[pstack-architect]], which plans in *code shapes* (types, signatures, `not implemented` bodies) rather than in prose. This is the wiki's clearest instance of a framework putting its rigor entirely downstream of specification. - **A new pattern: [[pattern-candidate-grafting]].** [[pstack-arena]] fans out N attempts at the same artifact, picks a base, and then **harvests the losers** for the one or two ideas worth porting in. Everyone else's competing-candidates step discards the non-winners ([[gstack-design-shotgun]], [[mp-prototype]]); treating them as a parts bin is new here. - **A new pattern: [[pattern-tooling-leverage]].** *"Build the tool that does it or proves it… **the tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun**."* The second clause is the contribution: the lever exists so a reviewer can re-derive the result, which is what makes it evidence rather than efficiency. - **A new pattern: [[pattern-idempotent-operations]].** Long-horizon agent work is interrupted constantly, so re-enterable steps are the precondition for [[pattern-autonomous-loop]] and [[pattern-session-handoff]] rather than an implementation nicety. - **A new artifact: [[artifact-decision-log]].** Every other durable artifact here is read by the *next agent* or by *future work*. [[pstack-show-me-your-work]]'s append-only TSV is read by **a human who was not watching**, so they can find the point where trust should stop. - **Suspension paged as its own procedure.** The mode skill carries a *Pause safely* playbook as the explicit complement of *Session pickup* — suspending in-flight work cleanly on an explicit pause, going offline, a restart, or imminent context compaction. Other frameworks page resumption ([[gstack-context-restore]], [[pstack-recall]]); pstack is the first to page the shutdown half. ## Signature mechanisms - **The sticky mode.** [[pstack-poteto-mode]] is `mode: true` with a `reminder` the harness re-injects every turn, so once entered it persists across turns and applies itself when a playbook matches or the task needs rigor. Every *other* skill in the plugin carries `disable-model-invocation: true`. The result is an inversion of [[superpowers]]' design, which makes every leaf auto-trigger — pstack makes the **router** persistent and every leaf explicitly manual, so there is exactly one thing deciding what fires. - **Playbooks copied in verbatim.** 23 playbook files, and the matched one's steps are copied into a todo list *verbatim* before any task-specific todos, with a skipped step staying in the list carrying a one-line `skip: `. Step text stays out of the router's context until needed, and skipping leaves a trace. - **The evidence ladder.** [[pstack-blast-radius]] grades every safety claim from *"you said so"* (worthless) through *pointed at the line*, *showed the bad case cannot happen*, *ran it*, up to *reproduced it in the running app* — and requires the writeup to **say where it stopped**, marking anything below rung 4 as **unproven**. The most operational form of [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]] in the wiki. - **The organizational-evidence sweep.** [[pstack-why]] discovers available MCP servers at run time and fans out one investigator per evidence category across source control, the issue tracker, long-form docs, team chat, infrastructure observability, error tracking, and the analytics warehouse, with shipped per-source playbooks and a rule that **a null result is a finding**. [[pstack-recall]] reuses the same machinery re-pointed at *current state*. No other framework here treats the organizational record as a first-class research corpus. - **Self-limiting rigor.** Several capabilities exist partly to say when *not* to apply themselves. [[pstack-tdd]] opens by listing when to skip the test and defines what a bad test is (*"prefer no new test over a bad test"*). [[pstack-how]] says *"when in doubt, take the simple path."* [[pstack-figure-it-out]] scales the evidence burden to blast radius. [[pstack-reflect]] skips trivial conversations because *"one-offs are not learnings."* This is [[pattern-scale-adaptive-planning]] applied to rigor rather than to ceremony. - **The comment-as-bug-report loop.** [[pstack-comment-sicko]] flags a comment on our own code as `MUST KILL` on the guilty *symbol*, and [[pstack-no-comments]] then implements the rename, extract, type, or reshape that makes the behavior obvious without prose — or, for a genuine constraint, **offers the cheapest type, runtime, test, or CI encoding and deletes the comment once it lands**. [[pstack-principle-encode-lessons-in-structure|Encoding lessons in structure]] run at the granularity of one line. - **Structural enforcement as a growth gate.** [[pstack-reflect]] re-reads its own synthesizer's Accepted list and **demotes to Backlog any learning better served by a lint rule, script, metadata flag, or runtime check**. The framework has a built-in brake on accreting prose, which is the failure mode most skill libraries drift into. - **A dormant automation pack.** **benny** ships inert inside the plugin — not registered as slash skills — and is installed per repository ([[pstack-benny-setup]]). It triages Slack issue reports ([[pstack-benny-triage]]) and reproduces confirmed bugs through the real UI before opening a **bounded draft PR** ([[pstack-benny-reproduce-and-fix]]). Both fail closed on incomplete configuration. It is the wiki's first example of capabilities triggered by an **external report rather than a developer's prompt**, and it is deliberately high-autonomy and low-authority. ## Capabilities by stage ### Align — understand before acting ([[stage-align]]) - [[pstack-how]] — how does X work; scale-adaptive parallel explorers then one synthesizing explainer. - [[pstack-why]] — why it is shaped this way; run-time MCP discovery, seven evidence categories in parallel, an explicit epistemics contract. - [[pstack-benny-triage]] — unattended Slack issue-report triage with cause-aware routing and fail-closed ticketing (intake flavor). ### Plan — settle the shape ([[stage-plan]]) - [[pstack-architect]] — types, signatures, and module boundaries before code; arena-driven sketch, design red-flag screen, and an explicit scrap phase. - [[pstack-figure-it-out]] — design a bespoke auditable playbook when none fits; falsifiable done predicate, rigor biased high, harness before work. ### Implement — write it ([[stage-implement]]) - [[pstack-tdd]] — failing test first where the path is cheap, with an explicit doctrine for when to skip. - [[pstack-recall]] — rebuild working context from your own chats *and* the shared organizational record before resuming. - [[pstack-typescript-best-practices]] — the only `paths:`-attached skill; grounds type-system discipline in syntax. - [[pstack-benny-reproduce-and-fix]] — unattended repro through the real UI, then a bounded draft PR after before-and-after proof. ### Review — judge it ([[stage-review]]) - [[pstack-interrogate]] — one reviewer per model, same prompt and rubric; diversity from models, not personas. - [[pstack-blast-radius]] — what this breaks elsewhere; find the one fact it is safe because of and prove it by running code. - [[pstack-no-comments]] — act on Comment Sicko's findings; root-cause fixes in scope, encodings for claimed constraints. - [[pstack-comment-sicko]] — the read-only comment reviewer (sub-agent). ### Validate — prove it works ([[stage-validate]]) - [[pstack-create-verification-skill]] — generate a project-local harness that drives the real app, any language or platform. - [[pstack-maintain-verification-skill]] — the upkeep loop; source wave plus one live pass, at most one PR of proven corrections. ### Learn — fold it back ([[stage-learn]]) - [[pstack-reflect]] — three parallel review lenses over the transcript, routed to concrete skill edits, gated by a structural-enforcement check. - [[pstack-automate-me]] — mine your transcripts into your own `-mode` skill; the framework's offer to be replaced as the entry point. - [[pstack-teach]] — explain a subsystem so a person understands it; diagram by diagram, no pedagogy theater. ### Cross-cutting — parallelism, prose, and setup (no single lifecycle stage) - [[pstack-poteto-mode]] — the sticky router; 23 playbooks and the inline principles index. - [[pstack-poteto-agent]] — the style-preserving subagent for any delegate inside a playbook step. - [[pstack-arena]] — N attempts at one artifact, pick a base, graft the losers. - [[pstack-swarm]] — N parallel cloud workers across slices or races, one aggregated report. - [[pstack-show-me-your-work]] — the append-only decision trail for unattended work. - [[pstack-unslop]] — cut AI tells; must always apply, with stable rule ids sibling skills cite. - [[pstack-technical-writing]] — Diátaxis + Google developer style + STE + Global English, layered. - [[pstack-bro]] — restate the last message in plain human language. - [[pstack-setup-pstack]] — map each role to a model; writes an always-applied rule, idempotently. - [[pstack-make-bot-ui]] — a page whose buttons wake a bot over a webhook, with the sender key kept server-side. - [[pstack-benny-setup]] — install and configure the dormant benny automation pack into a repository. ### The 23 principles Each is a loadable one-rule skill. [[pstack-poteto-mode]] indexes them inline and reads the index at task start; a leaf is read in full only when applied. **Core** - [[pstack-principle-laziness-protocol]] — bias to deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem. - [[pstack-principle-foundational-thinking]] — get the data structures right so downstream code becomes obvious. - [[pstack-principle-redesign-from-first-principles]] — redesign as if the requirement had been foundational, not bolted on. - [[pstack-principle-attack-the-premise]] — when two fixes sharing a premise fail the same gate, question the premise. - [[pstack-principle-subtract-before-you-add]] — remove dead weight first, then build on the simpler base. - [[pstack-principle-minimize-reader-load]] — count layers and hidden state; collapse one-caller wrappers. - [[pstack-principle-outcome-oriented-execution]] — converge on the target architecture, no throwaway compatibility states. - [[pstack-principle-experience-first]] — user delight over implementation convenience; fewer polished features. - [[pstack-principle-exhaust-the-design-space]] — 2-3 competing prototypes compared side by side before committing. - [[pstack-principle-build-the-lever]] — build the tool that does or proves it; the tool is what a reviewer reruns. **Architecture** - [[pstack-principle-model-the-domain]] — encode the domain in a structure, not scattered conditionals. - [[pstack-principle-boundary-discipline]] — guards at system boundaries, pure business logic inside. - [[pstack-principle-type-system-discipline]] — make illegal states unrepresentable; parse at boundaries. - [[pstack-principle-make-operations-idempotent]] — converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs. - [[pstack-principle-migrate-callers-then-delete-legacy-apis]] — migrate and delete in one wave. - [[pstack-principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state]] — eliminate the sharing before serializing it. **Verification** - [[pstack-principle-prove-it-works]] — verify against the real artifact, not a proxy or "it compiles". - [[pstack-principle-fix-root-causes]] — trace each symptom to its root cause and fix it there. - [[pstack-principle-sequence-verifiable-units]] — units that each end in a check, ordered so the sequence proves itself. - [[pstack-principle-test-behavior-not-implementation]] — if it passes when every import returns `undefined`, rewrite or delete it. **Delegation** - [[pstack-principle-guard-the-context-window]] — route bulk to subagents, keep summaries in the main thread. - [[pstack-principle-never-block-on-the-human]] — proceed on reversible work; pause only for irreversible writes. **Meta** - [[pstack-principle-encode-lessons-in-structure]] — encode the rule as a lint, flag, check, or script instead of more text. ## Harness gap: Cursor pstack runs on **Cursor**, and only on Cursor. There is no `wiki/harness/cursor.md` yet, so per the [support-scope rule](../CONVENTIONS.md#the-harness-layer) the `runs_on:` edge is left empty rather than pointed at a non-existent target, and the support is recorded here in prose. This is the first framework in the wiki with an empty `runs_on:`, and the gap is tracked in [log.md](../log.md). The source is unusually rich harness evidence should Cursor be ingested later: plugin manifests with `skills:` and `agents:` roots, `SKILL.md` frontmatter (`disable-model-invocation`, `mode: true` with `reminder`/`icon`/`color`, `paths:` auto-attach), `.mdc` rules with `alwaysApply`, the `Task` subagent surface (`subagent_type`, per-call `model`, `readonly`, `run_in_background`, `environment: cloud | local`, `cloud_base_branch`), MCP discovery, webhook routines, plan mode, `/loop`, the `cursor/plugins` marketplace, and transcripts on disk at `~/.cursor/projects//agent-transcripts/`. Two further Cursor-shipped plugins are referenced but not bundled: `cursor-team-kit` (which ships `/deslop`, `control-cli`, and `control-ui`) and Cursor's built-ins `/create-skill` and `/babysit`. ## Artifacts produced - [[artifact-decision-log]] — **new** — the append-only TSV decision trail ([[pstack-show-me-your-work]], [[pstack-figure-it-out]]). - [[artifact-review-report]] — review findings ([[pstack-interrogate]], [[pstack-blast-radius]], [[pstack-no-comments]], [[pstack-comment-sicko]]). - [[artifact-skill-doc]] — generated and edited skills ([[pstack-create-verification-skill]], [[pstack-automate-me]], [[pstack-reflect]]). - [[artifact-explainer]] — the understanding output ([[pstack-how]], [[pstack-why]], [[pstack-teach]]). - [[artifact-architecture]] · [[artifact-adr]] — the synthesized design package and its rationale ([[pstack-architect]]). - [[artifact-pull-request]] — the bounded draft PR ([[pstack-benny-reproduce-and-fix]]) and the maintenance PR ([[pstack-maintain-verification-skill]]). - [[artifact-issue]] — the deduplicated tracker item ([[pstack-benny-triage]]). - [[artifact-diataxis-docs]] · [[artifact-standards]] — the layered writing standard and the model-role rule ([[pstack-technical-writing]], [[pstack-typescript-best-practices]], [[pstack-setup-pstack]]). - [[artifact-handoff-doc]] — the current-state brief ([[pstack-recall]]). - [[artifact-plan-md]] — the designed phase list ([[pstack-figure-it-out]]). Notably **no spec artifact at all**. ## Patterns applied - [[pattern-cross-model-review]] — **signature** — model diversity as the review mechanism, and multi-model routing throughout ([[pstack-interrogate]], [[pstack-arena]], [[pstack-architect]], [[pstack-reflect]], [[pstack-setup-pstack]]). - [[pattern-candidate-grafting]] — **new, signature** — bakeoff then harvest the losers ([[pstack-arena]], [[pstack-architect]]). - [[pattern-tooling-leverage]] — **new, signature** — build the lever a reviewer can rerun ([[pstack-principle-build-the-lever]], [[pstack-create-verification-skill]], [[pstack-blast-radius]]). - [[pattern-idempotent-operations]] — **new** — converge regardless of partial prior runs ([[pstack-principle-make-operations-idempotent]], [[pstack-setup-pstack]], [[pstack-benny-setup]]). - [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]] — **co-signature** — the five-rung evidence ladder and the VERIFIED / NOT VERIFIED / **INCONCLUSIVE** verdict where *inconclusive is not a pass* ([[pstack-blast-radius]], [[pstack-figure-it-out]], [[pstack-principle-prove-it-works]]). - [[pattern-context-engineering]] — bulk stays in subagents, only findings reach the parent; *do not paste raw worker dumps* ([[pstack-how]], [[pstack-recall]], [[pstack-swarm]]). - [[pattern-fresh-context-subagents]] — with a twist: the style-preserving [[pstack-poteto-agent]] exists precisely because a *generic* fresh subagent drifts. - [[pattern-wave-parallelism]] — fan-outs everywhere ([[pstack-swarm]], [[pstack-arena]], [[pstack-how]], [[pstack-reflect]], [[pstack-maintain-verification-skill]]). - [[pattern-worktree-isolation]] — every fan-out gives each worker its own worktree or output path ([[pstack-principle-separate-before-serializing-shared-state]]). - [[pattern-scale-adaptive-planning]] — rigor, not ceremony, sized to blast radius ([[pstack-figure-it-out]], [[pstack-how]], [[pstack-poteto-mode]]). - [[pattern-deep-modules]] — the Ousterhout red-flag screen: shallow modules, information leakage, temporal decomposition, pass-through methods ([[pstack-architect]]). - [[pattern-contract-first]] — the data shape named before any code; parse at the boundary ([[pstack-principle-model-the-domain]], [[pstack-typescript-best-practices]]). - [[pattern-source-grounding]] — pointed at the **organizational** record rather than the public one ([[pstack-why]], [[pstack-recall]]). - [[pattern-knowledge-compounding]] — transcripts mined into skill edits and personal mode skills ([[pstack-reflect]], [[pstack-automate-me]]). - [[pattern-adversarial-review]] — *"tear this apart"* ([[pstack-interrogate]], [[pstack-comment-sicko]]). - [[pattern-autonomous-loop]] — the Autonomous run, Orchestrate, and both Autopilot playbooks; benny's unattended fix loop. - [[pattern-session-handoff]] — Session pickup **and** Pause safely, plus [[pstack-recall]]'s two-record reconstruction. - [[pattern-systematic-debugging]] — root cause before fix, escalating to [[pstack-principle-attack-the-premise]] when fixes sharing a premise keep failing. - [[pattern-test-driven-development]] — present but deliberately conditional ([[pstack-tdd]]). - [[pattern-deterministic-gates]] — the structural-enforcement check, the `PASS`/`ISSUES`/`BLOCKED` worker contract, the clean/changed/blocked outcome declaration. - [[pattern-persona-agents]] — used in exactly one place, and the framework argues against it everywhere else ([[pstack-comment-sicko]]). - [[pattern-throwaway-prototype]] — the Prototype playbook, and prototyping as the answer to a question the human should not be asked. ## See Also - [[superpowers]] — the closest structural cousin and the sharpest contrast. Settles the shape before writing code. It sketches types, function signatures, class shapes, and module boundaries with `not implemented` bodies and pseudocode, synthesizes across multiple model perspectives, then fills in code against the chosen sketch. [[pstack-poteto-mode]] fires it on any code crossing a function boundary. Five phases, opened as a todo list before anything starts. - **A. Ground.** Build a real mental model of every system the new code touches by running [[pstack-how]] over the relevant subsystems. *Naming a file is not grounding* — produce the traced model `how` prescribes. If the design redefines ownership or layering, also run [[pstack-why]] on the existing shape so the rationale becomes a constraint rather than a guess. Skipped only for genuinely greenfield work. - **B. Sketch.** Run [[pstack-arena]] with the design-sketch task, one candidate per configured architect runner across four different models. **Design it twice** — at least two *structurally distinct* candidates are required before synthesis, even when the first looks sufficient, and they must be whole-shape alternatives rather than point fixes inside one shape. Every candidate is screened against a shipped `design-red-flags.md` and rejected or revised for **shallow modules, information leakage, temporal decomposition, and pass-through methods**. Surviving candidates are compared on **interface depth**: prefer the design that hides more complexity behind a smaller, simpler public surface. - **C. Agree.** Opt-in only. The default is to proceed straight to implementation with no human checkpoint, per [[pstack-principle-never-block-on-the-human]]. The synthesized sketch may ship as its own commit either way — the scaffold-first mode of [[pstack-principle-foundational-thinking]]. For adversarial pressure before implementing, run [[pstack-interrogate]] on the sketch. - **D. Implement against the sketch.** The synthesized sketch is the contract. **Deviations are signal worth surfacing, not friction to absorb silently** — a function needing a parameter the sketch did not anticipate raises the question of whether the sketch was wrong, the requirement was missed, or the implementation is overreaching. - **E. Scrap.** When implementation keeps producing friction the sketch cannot absorb, throw the sketch out rather than bolting fixes onto a wrong design. The signal is a *pattern*, not single instances, and the tells are listed: the same shape of workaround recurring across unrelated code, multiple unrelated edge cases each needing a special-case branch, types needing escape hatches (`any`, casts, optional fields always set in practice) to compile, the "we need a lock" reflex when the sketch said the state was not shared, callers having to know the abstraction's internal rules, and two or more independent Phase D deviations of the same shape. Phases B and E are what separate it from the wiki's other design capabilities. The red-flag screen is a direct import of Ousterhout's design vocabulary, making this the sharpest [[pattern-deep-modules]] instance here alongside [[mp-codebase-design]]; and the scrap phase pages *abandoning* a design as a named step with falsifiable triggers, which no other framework does. ## See Also - [[pstack-arena]] — the fan-out engine Phase B runs on. - [[pstack-how]] · [[pstack-why]] — the Phase A grounding. - [[pstack-interrogate]] — optional adversarial pressure on the synthesized sketch. - [[mp-codebase-design]] — the deep-modules counterpart; [[gstack-plan-eng-review]] — the eng-manager architecture lock. - [[stage-plan]] — the canonical stage this implements. ## [2026-09-11] ingest | pstack — the anti-spec pole, and rigor as the precondition for parallelism - Source: Lauren Tan (poteto — React core team, Cursor), **pstack v0.15.2**, `github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack`, MIT → `raw/pstack/2026-09-11-pstack-plugin.md` (plugin.json manifest, full README, the `poteto-mode` SKILL.md verbatim, generated frontmatter catalogue of all 48 skills and agents including the benny pack, benny README, full file tree). Fetched by sparse-checkout of the `cursor/plugins` monorepo. - **Layer call: `framework`** — CONVENTIONS §0. It ships an opinionated methodology across the lifecycle (align → learn) as an installable capability set, not an agent loop, not something that spawns loops, not durable state. Stage coverage confirms it: six of eight stages carry real capabilities. - **52 capability pages, full coverage** per the standing preference: 25 skills, 23 principle skills (`pstack-principle-*`), 2 subagents, 3 benny automation skills. The 23 playbooks are documented on [[pstack-poteto-mode]] rather than paged individually — they are steps copied into a todo list, not invocable units, so they fail the "unit of work a framework exposes" test. - **Three new patterns minted.** [[pattern-candidate-grafting]] (run N attempts at one artifact, pick a base, then **harvest the losers** — the variant of [[pattern-throwaway-prototype]] that does not discard, and distinct from [[pattern-cross-model-review]] in that each model produces a *whole* artifact); [[pattern-tooling-leverage]] (build the lever, and specifically ***the tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun*** — the constructive complement of [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]]); [[pattern-idempotent-operations]] (ordinary ops discipline that earns a node here because agent runs are interrupted constantly, making it the precondition for [[pattern-autonomous-loop]] and [[pattern-session-handoff]]). Each is single-framework for now, which the pattern layer allows — the ≥2-framework bar governs *stages*, not patterns — and each is cross-linked from the neighbours it is easily confused with. - **One new artifact: [[artifact-decision-log]].** The append-only TSV trail from [[pstack-show-me-your-work]]. Minted because its **reader** is new: every other durable artifact here is read by the next agent ([[artifact-handoff-doc]], the store layer) or by future work ([[artifact-retrospective]], [[artifact-solution-doc]]); this one is read by a human who was not watching, so they can locate the point where trust should stop. ## Cross-framework equivalents
The **finalize / close-out** cluster spans five frameworks: OpenSpec's [[openspec-archive]] ↔ Addy's [[addy-shipping]] ↔ GSD's [[gsd-ship]] ↔ Compound Engineering's [[ce-commit-push-pr]] ↔ Superpowers' [[sp-finishing-a-development-branch]] — each closes the iteration on a completed unit, but finalizes *different things*: GSD opens and tracks a PR, Addy fans out parallel review personas for a go/no-go launch, Compound Engineering goes working-changes→PR and (with [[ce-promote]]) announces the launch, OpenSpec merges the spec delta and archives the change, and Superpowers presents a **merge/PR/keep/discard decision menu** and cleans up its worktree accordingly (like GSD and OpenSpec, it stops at PR/merge with **no deploy step**). Addy's other five capabilities (versioning, CI/CD, observability, docs, deprecation) still have **no counterpart** in GSD, MP, OpenSpec, Spec Kit, or BMAD; OpenSpec's spec-maintenance is unique. Compound Engineering is the closest match to the GSD/Addy ship-to-prod flavor. (These are *not* set as `equivalent_to` edges: the terminal acts differ too much to cluster as counterparts.) The former **learning close-out** flavor ([[bmad-retrospective]]) now lives in [[stage-learn]], alongside Compound Engineering's [[ce-compound]].

> **Spec Kit ships no release capability (2026-07-04).** Like OpenSpec, Spec Kit stops at the validate loop: [[speckit-converge]] closes the spec↔code gap by re-planning, but there is no deploy / PR / launch / observability command. Its [[speckit-taskstoissues]] pushes tasks to GitHub issues (a [[stage-plan]] tracker bridge), not a release act. So Spec Kit adds no backlink here.

## Split candidates

### stage-operate / stage-maintain (deploy, run it in production, sunset it) — strengthening
- **Distinction:** *release* = ship the work (PR/merge); *operate* = deploy it and keep it healthy in production (deploy, verify, observability, alerting); *maintain* = retire/migrate it later. Distinct from opening/merging the PR.
- **Evidence so far (now capability-level in three frameworks, but not yet a distinct *phase*):**
  - Addy folds observability ([[addy-observability]]), CI/CD ([[addy-ci-cd]]), and deprecation ([[addy-deprecation]]) into Ship.
  - Compound Engineering adds post-release monitoring ([[ce-product-pulse]]).
  - **gstack (2026-07-05) is the first to give deploy its own command** ([[gstack-land-and-deploy]]) *separate from* ship, plus a dedicated post-deploy monitor ([[gstack-canary]]) and deploy config ([[gstack-setup-deploy]]) — a genuine deploy→operate arc. But gstack still nests these under the release/ship end of its sprint rather than naming a standalone *Operate* phase.
  - So deploy+operate is now a **dedicated capability in three frameworks** (Addy, CE, gstack) but a distinct *phase* in none.
- **Decisive trigger:** a framework that treats **operate/deploy as its own lifecycle phase** distinct from release (or a second framework separating deploy into its own command + phase) → clears the bar → split into `stage-operate`. Watch closely — gstack has brought this from one framework to three at the capability level.

# SDLC Stages

*Index — the eight canonical stages, in execution order.*

The eight **canonical, framework-neutral lifecycle stages** synthesized across the frameworks in this wiki. Each is a **derived projection** — its content comes from the capabilities that `implements:` it (see [CONVENTIONS.md](../CONVENTIONS.md) for the ontology). Listed below in the order they typically execute.

The lifecycle is a **loop, not a line**: the last stage ([Learn](stage-learn.md)) feeds its output back into the front ([Align](stage-align.md)) so each iteration starts ahead of the last.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A([1 · Align]) --> S([2 · Specify])
    S --> P([3 · Plan])
    P --> I([4 · Implement])
    I --> V([5 · Validate])
    I --> R([6 · Review])
    V --> Rel([7 · Release])
    R --> Rel
    Rel --> L([8 · Learn])
    L -. grounds the next iteration .-> A
```

| # | Stage | The question it answers | Framework terms it subsumes (`aka`) |

### Off-stage capabilities

The **12 capabilities** that map to no lifecycle stage — cross-cutting tooling that runs *around* the pipeline rather than advancing it. Grouped by kind:

- **Routing / dispatch & bootstrap** — the one near-universal off-stage capability (four frameworks, all `equivalent_to`-linked): [[addy-using-agent-skills]], [[mp-ask-matt]], [[gstack-router]], [[sp-using-superpowers]] ("which skill fits?" meta-skills; the Superpowers one doubles as the mandatory-skill-invocation bootstrap).
- **Session & context continuity** — [[mp-handoff]] (compact a conversation into a handoff doc so a fresh session resumes without re-deriving context). *(gstack's [[gstack-context-save]] / [[gstack-context-restore]] do the same job but the wiki files them under Implement.)*
- **Spec-pack state ops** — [[nano-spec-status]], [[nano-spec-update]] (report on / mutate an existing [[artifact-nano-spec-pack|nano-spec pack]] rather than advancing a step).
- **Publishing & diagrams** — [[gstack-diagram]] (Diagram Maker), [[gstack-make-pdf]] (markdown → publication-quality PDF).
- **Tooling & self-maintenance** — [[gstack-benchmark-models]] (cross-model benchmark of gstack's own skills), [[gstack-upgrade]] (self-updater), [[bm-favicon-creator]] (favicon asset generator).

**The pattern:** the five frameworks that *own the whole process* (GSD, OpenSpec, Spec Kit, BMAD, Compound Engineering) keep **everything** on the lifecycle — zero off-stage capabilities. The toolkit / marketplace-style ones (gstack, Matt Pocock, nano-spec, BM Skills — and Addy/Superpowers with their routers) ship standalone utilities alongside the pipeline. gstack alone accounts for 5 of the 12, consistent with it being the largest, most "virtual-engineering-team" framework here.

<sup>†</sup> OpenSpec's Release is a **spec-merge** (`archive`), not a code deploy — gstack is the only framework here with a genuine deploy step. Folded (🔗) cases: GSD, Superpowers, and Compound Engineering capture the *what* inside Align/Plan rather than a separate spec; OpenSpec bundles design + task-decomposition into its `propose` (specify) step. BM Skills and nano-spec are deliberately point tools, not full-SDLC frameworks.

## Stores on the stage map

The matrix above is **framework × stage**, and the [store layer](../store/index.md) is deliberately not in it. A store holds durable work state; running *around* the lifecycle rather than advancing it is what it is for, so scoring one against eight stages would rank it low for succeeding at its job. Two stores nonetheless ship some genuine lifecycle work, listed here so the evidence stays visible without competing with framework rows:

| Store | On-stage | Off-stage | What it implements |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[seeds]] | 14 of 37 | 23 | [[stage-plan]] — the whole `sd plan` surface (templated, AJV-gated, spawns the children) plus filing and dependency-wiring; [[stage-learn]] — [[seeds-plan-outcome]], a storage-only stub |
| [[beads]] | 1 of 51 | 50 | [[stage-plan]] — [[beads-mol]] alone, pouring a formula into dependency-ordered work |

The gap between the two rows is the layer's own open argument, not a quality difference. Beads' charter **forbids** carrying methodology — *"the orchestration layer owns […] workflow semantics"* — so its single on-stage capability is deliberate minimalism, and even that one is template instantiation rather than reasoning. Seeds bakes a planning methodology into the store so that the plan and the queue are one object. The rest of the contrast is in the [store matrix](../store/index.md#the-comparison-matrix).

**What this means for the rosters:** a `Seeds:` or `Beads:` group under [[stage-plan]] is store evidence, and it is weaker evidence for a *stage* than a framework's — a store implements a stage as a side effect of holding state about it, where a framework implements it on purpose. Weight it accordingly during [re-derivation](../CONVENTIONS.md#stage-re-derivation-keep-stages-framework-neutral); in particular, a candidate stage evidenced by two stores and no framework has not cleared the bar.

# Pattern: Idempotent operations

Design commands, lifecycle steps, and processing loops to **converge to the same end state regardless of partial prior runs**. Re-running is always safe; a crash, a restart, or a retry mid-way leaves no half-state the next run has to reason about.

This is classic operational engineering, but it acquires a specific edge in agent work, which is why it earns a pattern page here rather than staying an implementation detail. Agent runs are **interrupted far more often than human ones** — context compaction, a session ending, a killed subagent, a cloud worker dropping out, an operator pressing stop. Every long-horizon capability in this wiki therefore depends on its steps being re-enterable, and the frameworks that run unattended lean on it hardest. It is the precondition that makes [[pattern-autonomous-loop]] and [[pattern-session-handoff]] safe: a resumed session can re-run the last step rather than having to determine exactly how far the dead one got.

Its most visible expression is a setup or configuration command that **overwrites its whole output** rather than patching it, so a second run cannot accumulate drift from the first.

## Applied by (backlinks)

pstack:

- [[pstack-principle-make-operations-idempotent]] — the principle statement, scoped to commands, lifecycle steps, and loops that run amid crashes and retries.
- [[pstack-setup-pstack]] — overwrites the whole model-role rule file on every run so re-runs stay idempotent.
- [[pstack-benny-setup]] — a re-runnable install that preserves destination-only files and reviews conflicts instead of overwriting local edits.

Tessl:

- [[tessl-environment]] — an update **replaces** an environment's values rather than merging them, so a re-run converges on exactly the supplied set. Safety over convenience, and the right default for a secret store.
- [[tessl-schedule]] — recurring unattended runs, which only make sense if each run is safe to repeat.

## See Also
- [[pattern-autonomous-loop]] — long unattended runs depend on their steps being re-enterable.
- [[pattern-session-handoff]] — resumption is cheap when re-running a step is free.
- [[pattern-deterministic-gates]] — both make a run's outcome independent of how it got there.

7:A wave of open-source "agent frameworks" appeared through 2026: GSD, Spec Kit, BMAD, OpenSpec, Superpowers, gstack, Compound Engineering, Agent OS, pstack and others. Each ships a bundle of slash-commands, skills, and sub-agents that walk a coding agent from a vague idea to merged code. They use different vocabulary, disagree about ceremony, and are mostly documented only by their own READMEs — so it is genuinely hard to tell whether two of them are doing the same thing under different names.
9:This wiki reads them side by side. Every framework is decomposed into its individual capabilities, each capability is tagged with the lifecycle stage it performs and the techniques it applies, and matching capabilities across frameworks are linked to one another. What emerges from those links — rather than from anyone's opinion — is a **canonical eight-stage lifecycle** and a set of recurring **patterns** that most frameworks independently converged on.
11:It currently covers **13 frameworks**, **391 capabilities**, **40 artifacts**, **37 patterns**, **4 agent harnesses**, **5 execution runtimes**, **2 state stores**, and **1 capability registry**.
17:- **Process layer** — a **[framework](catalogue.md#framework)** ships **[capabilities](catalogue.md#capability)** (commands, skills, sub-agents). Each capability performs one canonical **[sdlc-stage](catalogue.md#sdlc-stage)**, produces **[artifacts](catalogue.md#artifact)**, and applies **[patterns](catalogue.md#pattern)**.
20:- **[Store](catalogue.md#store) layer** — the durable work graph and memory that outlives any single run, so a session that ends or crashes does not take the work with it. The framework, harness and runtime layers are compute and are gone when the run ends; this is the one that survives.
21:- **[Registry](catalogue.md#registry) layer** — the versioned index capabilities are discovered in, scanned, scored, evaluated and installed from, *before* any run begins. Where a store holds what a run produced, a registry holds what a run was provisioned from.
23:Two page types are derived rather than authored. **Stage** pages are synthesised purely from the capabilities that link to them — they are evidence summaries, not opinions, and get re-derived on every ingest so the stage names stay neutral rather than borrowing one framework's branding. **[Topic](catalogue.md#topic)** pages are the opposite: hand-written essays that cut across everything else.
29:**Choosing a framework.** Start at the **[framework catalogue](catalogue.md#framework)**. Each entry states the framework's shape, its signature idea, which stages it covers and which it skips, and how heavy it is. Useful contrasts: [Spec Kit](framework/speckit.md) (gated, maximalist, the reference spec-driven implementation) vs [nano-spec](framework/nano-spec.md) (four tiny files) vs [Superpowers](framework/superpowers.md) (a complete methodology from 14 auto-triggering skills) vs [Agent OS](framework/agent-os.md) (deliberately owns only the front of the lifecycle) vs [pstack](framework/pstack.md) (ships no spec step at all and puts every gram of its rigor into verification and review). If none of them fit because what you actually lack is durable state rather than a methodology, the answer is a layer down: see the [store layer](store/index.md).
31:**Borrowing one good idea instead of adopting a whole framework.** Most teams don't want another methodology; they want the two or three moves that actually work. Browse the **[capability catalogue](catalogue.md#capability)** or a **[stage](catalogue.md#sdlc-stage)** page, find the cluster of frameworks solving the same problem, and take the best-shaped version. Cross-framework counterparts are linked on every page.
33:**Deciding how much process you actually want.** The collection now spans the full range, and the poles are worth reading against each other. [Spec Kit](framework/speckit.md) and [OpenSpec](framework/openspec.md) front-load a written contract and gate everything against it; [pstack](framework/pstack.md) argues the opposite case in its own README — *"i don't believe in planning, the best spec is code"* — and instead spends its rigor downstream on graded evidence, multi-model review, and generated verification harnesses. Neither is the consensus; the disagreement about **where in the lifecycle rigor belongs** is one of the more useful things visible only when these tools are read side by side.
35:**Finding the high-confidence practices.** The **[pattern](catalogue.md#pattern)** pages record how many independent frameworks converged on each technique. A pattern shared by eight frameworks that never talked to each other is a much stronger signal than any single project's README — that is the main thing this wiki produces that reading the sources individually cannot.
41:**Rolling this out across an organization.** The community frameworks assume one motivated engineer; **[the AI-native SDLC](topic/topic-ai-native-sdlc.md)** covers the org-level view — Anthropic's own enterprise playbook (committed artifact chain, advisory-skill/deterministic-hook controls, governance enforced as the agent acts) read against the wiki's stages and patterns, with the convergences and the one instrument nobody else ships noted.
43:**Managing skills at organizational scale.** Every framework here encourages writing more skills, and none of them manages the corpus that results — which is why a commercial layer has grown to do it. The **[registry layer](registry/index.md)** covers capability distribution as a supply chain: versioning and rollback, security scanning of instructions ([[pattern-supply-chain-scanning]]), measuring whether a skill actually changes agent behavior ([[pattern-capability-evals]]), org-wide inventory, RBAC and install policy. Read it if your problem is no longer *which skills should we write* but *which of the two hundred we have are any good, and who is allowed to install them*.
49:**Getting oriented in the field.** Read [CONVENTIONS](CONVENTIONS.md) for the vocabulary, then any two framework pages. The **[visual artifact index](artifact/index.md)** shows how the documents these tools produce flow into one another across a whole lifecycle.
53:Every article is compiled from captured primary sources — each framework's own documentation and source, archived unmodified before compilation. Pages cite what they were built from and when. The change history, including the reasoning behind every schema decision and stage rename, is in the **[log](log.md)**.

The guide says so in its first line: > "Factory skills install agent instructions. They do not add integrations, credentials, scheduled jobs, or permission grants. Host support and the configuration conventions can change." The pieces a runtime would own are all borrowed from the **host harness**: the scheduler (*"Every recurring job must be created and verified in the host scheduler"*), the connectors (*"there is no fixed Factory connector catalog"*), the worktree (`fresh-per-run` is a request that the host may not honour), and the credentials. Its configuration is *"an agent-readable convention, not a validated schema"*. The Factory is a methodology for running a factory that you assemble from whatever your harness already exposes. Stage coverage agrees: twelve of the 24 capabilities perform a lifecycle stage, and the Factory's own modules cover align, review, release, and learn. That makes it the wiki's first instance of the **prompt-owned control plane**. It is the opposite bet to [[sssf]], whose pitch is *"moving the control plane out of the prompt and into Python"*. In the software-factory grid, the control-plane column *"in the prompt — the agent sequences itself"* had no documented anchor until this ingest. See the [dated section on the topic page](../topic/topic-software-factory.md#a-factory-with-no-runtime-the-skill-pack-pole). ## Distinctive contributions to the ontology - **Authority decomposed into ten independent actions.** *"Fix, reply, close, review, approve, publish, merge, deploy, recover, and notify are independent decisions."* Each has its own policy (`never` · `manual` · `criteria` with `allow`/`stop` lists · `after-fix` / `after-merge` proof points), and the rule against inference is stated in every skill: *"The skills never infer permission for one action from another."* Other frameworks gate *whether* the agent may act ([[pattern-edit-guardrails]]) or *whether* the work is good ([[pattern-deterministic-gates]]). This one gates **each kind of external write separately**, which is why [[pattern-action-gating]] is minted here. [[pstack]]'s benny pack and [[gh-aw]]'s safe outputs were the two earlier instances. - **Evidence bound to the live head, with a soak.** Approval and merge evidence counts only for the exact head it was read against. *"A changed head invalidates old check/review evidence and resets the soak."* The soak is a configured unchanged interval (e.g. `10 minutes`) that the agent must actually observe: *"Missing history does not satisfy it."* This is the most precise statement in the wiki of *when* a gate result expires. - **Unavailable, truncated, and empty are three different answers.** Every Factory skill carries some form of *"A missing connector, partial page, or failed query is not an empty source"* and *"Never report 'no recurring issues' when coverage is partial."* It is [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]] applied to the agent's **inputs**, where the pattern usually targets its outputs, and it is what stops an unattended sweep over a broken connector from reporting all clear. - **The factory's front door is the user.** Intake here is product feedback, telemetry, and runtime errors, not a ticket queue. [[builder-factory-collect]] triages them, may ask the reporter **one targeted question** if the reply policy allows, and re-triages the original report when an answer comes back. [[pstack-benny-triage]] was the only earlier framework capability triggered by an external report. This is the first to make it a standing, scheduled workflow. - **Learning from production, not from the session.** [[builder-factory-lookback]] clusters a bounded history of reports, errors, and prior fixes. It asks why the same class of problem keeps coming back and prefers *"one verified correction at that boundary over a pile of caller-specific patches."* This is a **third flavor of [[stage-learn]]**. The existing two fold lessons into an agent corpus or a team retrospective; this one folds the product's own recurrence signal into a systemic fix. See the note on the stage page. - **The human is a queue, not an interrupt.** [[builder-factory-human-digest]] is a read-only, deduplicated list of everything the automated paths held for a person, including PRs awaiting judgment, reports held for context, and answers not yet re-triaged. It is the *escalation* socket in the [factory anatomy](../topic/topic-software-factory.md#anatomy-of-a-factory) implemented as a capability. The nearest earlier thing is [[beads]]' `bd human` in the store layer. - **Configuration you must read back.** *"A YAML schedule is only a request; `/factory` must read the saved job settings back and report anything the host could not configure."* The Factory treats its own setup the way it treats a PR: a claim is not proof until live state confirms it. - **Prompt overlays that cannot grant permission.** `skill_prompts.` layers project-specific text onto each module and is copied into saved automation prompts. It *"cannot override the user's current request, grant permission, or weaken repository and host safeguards"*, and on conflict *"follow the more restrictive requirement and surface the conflict."* - **A new artifact: [[artifact-autonomy-policy]].** `.agent-factory/config.yaml` is the durable, per-project document that says which actions the agent may take unattended and under what conditions. The nearest earlier artifacts are [[artifact-constitution]] (principles that gate plans) and [[artifact-standards]] (conventions). This one governs **authority** rather than design or style. ## The other skills The non-Factory skills share no workflow. Three themes group them, and a fourth group consists of product front-ends. - **Cross-agent review and autonomy.** [[builder-agent-watchdog]] audits another agent's run as a *second investigator* rather than a grader. [[builder-plan-arbiter]] turns competing plans from different agents into one decision memo. [[builder-plow-ahead]] is an explicit autonomy contract with named stop conditions and a closing decision recap. All three assume a user who runs **Codex and Claude Code side by side** and moves work between them. That multi-harness, multi-vendor workflow is taken as given here and is still unusual in this wiki. - **Cost-tiered orchestration.** [[builder-efficient-fable]] and [[builder-efficient-frontier]] keep the expensive model for judgment and send bounded, token-heavy work to cheaper subagents. [[builder-stay-within-limits]] checks 5-hour and weekly usage between waves and pauses at 95%. Together with [[pstack-setup-pstack]] and [[gsd]]'s Opus-tier planner, the first two are enough evidence to mint [[pattern-model-tiering]]. - **Discipline conventions.** [[builder-read-the-damn-docs]] requires reading the docs before writing code against external APIs. [[builder-quick-recap]] ends every response with a 🟢/🟡/🔴 status line. - **Agent-Native front-ends.** [[builder-visual-plan]], [[builder-visual-recap]], [[builder-visual-edit]], [[builder-an]], [[builder-webmcp]], [[builder-rewind]], and [[builder-turn-into-app]] each connect the agent to a Builder-hosted surface (Plans, Design, Dispatch-hosted apps, Clips Desktop screen memory) through MCP or in-page WebMCP tools. Their procedures are mostly about host integration. The ideas that carry over are **one read, one smallest mutation, one readback** (WebMCP), recaps that describe a diff *"at a higher altitude than line-by-line review"*, and plans published as commentable review surfaces instead of chat paragraphs. ## Capabilities by stage ### Align: understand before acting ([[stage-align]]) - [[builder-factory-collect]]: collect and triage configured feedback, telemetry, errors, and issues, with coverage accounting, and apply separate fix, reply, and close gates (intake flavor). ### Plan: settle the shape ([[stage-plan]]) - [[builder-plan-arbiter]]: cross-review competing agent plans, then adopt one, build a hybrid, or send them back for revision, returning a decision memo with an executor recommendation. - [[builder-visual-plan]]: publish the plan as an interactive, commentable MDX review surface with diagrams, file maps, and an optional wireframe or prototype. ### Implement: write it ([[stage-implement]]) - [[builder-read-the-damn-docs]]: a docs-first trigger list and workflow that requires web-searching official docs before coding against external contracts. - [[builder-visual-edit]]: open a running local app in hosted Design as route-backed screens and edit the source from the canvas. ### Review: judge it ([[stage-review]]) - [[builder-factory-review-prs]]: sweep a filtered PR queue; findings kept separate from reply, approval, and merge gates. - [[builder-agent-watchdog]]: audit another agent's work by running an independent investigation and diffing it against theirs. - [[builder-visual-recap]]: turn a diff into an interactive visual recap for reviewers; also available as a GitHub Action on every PR. ### Release: deliver it ([[stage-release]]) - [[builder-factory-ship]]: verify, publish, merge under a head-match guard, and **verify the deployment separately**, because *"a merge is not live proof."* - [[builder-factory-babysit-pr]]: follow one explicitly authorized PR through checks and review, fixing in-scope findings under six separate action gates including a soak. ### Learn: fold it back ([[stage-learn]]) - [[builder-factory-lookback]]: a bounded retrospective over production signal that looks for recurrence after a claimed fix and aims for one systemic change at the shared boundary. - [[builder-turn-into-app]]: package a proven thread, skill, or workflow into a runnable Agent-Native app. ### Cross-cutting: setup, supervision, autonomy, and tooling (no single lifecycle stage) **Factory control** - [[builder-factory]]: configure sources, ten independent action policies, overlays, schedules, and worktrees, and read back host automations. - [[builder-factory-human-digest]]: read-only queue of work held for human judgment, grouped by underlying pattern. - [[builder-factory-watchdog]]: find stalled, authorized delivery work and notify only when a concrete next step is due (`DONT_NOTIFY` otherwise). - [[builder-factory-recover]]: resume interrupted runs only while their original authorization and worktree are still valid, without repeating completed writes. **Autonomy and cost** - [[builder-plow-ahead]]: convert routine questions into stated assumptions, stop only for listed blockers, and end with an auditable decision recap. - [[builder-efficient-fable]]: Claude Fable as orchestrator and final judge, with cheaper subagents doing research, coding, and testing. - [[builder-efficient-frontier]]: the same orchestration for any high-cost frontier model. - [[builder-stay-within-limits]]: check the usage window between waves, pause at 95%, and resume from a self-contained wake prompt. - [[builder-quick-recap]]: the 🟢/🟡/🔴 end-of-response status line, installed as a managed `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` block. **Agent-Native surfaces** - [[builder-an]]: open and operate a granted Agent-Native app through Dispatch MCP (also the `/an` command). - [[builder-webmcp]]: open a URL in the host's built-in browser and use the page's WebMCP tools before any UI automation. - [[builder-rewind]]: retrieve recent local screen context from Clips Rewind, local-first, with permission-gated setup. ## Harness support The installer targets *"the shared `.agents` path for Codex, Pi, Cursor, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot / VS Code, and similar agents, plus Claude Code's native skills path"*. The repo also ships `.claude-plugin/` and `.codex-plugin/` manifests and a Cowork marketplace. Per the [support-scope rule](../CONVENTIONS.md#the-harness-layer), `runs_on:` is wired to the three that have pages: **claude-code**, **pi**, **opencode**. **Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot / VS Code, and Claude Cowork** are also officially supported and are recorded here as prose until they have pages. Cursor is now named by a fifth independent source (after [[pstack]], [[tessl]], [[beads]], and [[superpowers]]' harness list). ## Artifacts produced - [[artifact-autonomy-policy]]: **new**. The per-action authority document (`.agent-factory/config.yaml`) written by [[builder-factory]] and read by every Factory module. - [[artifact-pull-request]]: the gated PR ([[builder-factory-collect]], [[builder-factory-ship]], [[builder-factory-babysit-pr]]). - [[artifact-review-report]]: PR findings and gap reports ([[builder-factory-review-prs]], [[builder-agent-watchdog]]). - [[artifact-retrospective]]: the lookback report covering coverage, recurrence, confirmed cause, and systemic fix ([[builder-factory-lookback]]). - [[artifact-plan-md]]: the arbitrated execution plan and the visual plan ([[builder-plan-arbiter]], [[builder-visual-plan]]). - [[artifact-explainer]]: the visual recap of a diff ([[builder-visual-recap]]). - [[artifact-decision-log]]: the autonomous-decision recap, written for a human who was not watching ([[builder-plow-ahead]]). - [[artifact-handoff-doc]]: self-contained wake prompts and blocked-state handoffs ([[builder-stay-within-limits]], [[builder-plow-ahead]]). ## Patterns applied - [[pattern-action-gating]]: **new, signature**. Ten independently authorized actions, no inference between them, live-state recheck before each write ([[builder-factory]] and every Factory module). - [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]]: **co-signature**. Unavailable ≠ truncated ≠ empty, *"a merge is not live proof"*, and schedules that count only after read-back ([[builder-factory-collect]], [[builder-factory-lookback]], [[builder-factory-ship]], [[builder-factory]]). - [[pattern-deterministic-gates]]: head-bound check and review evidence with a soak interval that restarts on any change ([[builder-factory-babysit-pr]], [[builder-factory-review-prs]], [[builder-factory-ship]]). - [[pattern-autonomous-loop]]: host-scheduled collect, lookback, digest, and watchdog jobs; [[builder-plow-ahead]]'s autonomy contract. - [[pattern-worktree-isolation]]: `fresh-per-run` automation-owned worktrees, and *"keep the workflow manual rather than borrowing a shared checkout"* when the host cannot provide one. - [[pattern-model-tiering]]: **new**. Expensive model for judgment, cheap models for bounded heavy lifting ([[builder-efficient-fable]], [[builder-efficient-frontier]]). - [[pattern-cross-model-review]]: one vendor's agent auditing or arbitrating another's ([[builder-agent-watchdog]], [[builder-plan-arbiter]]). - [[pattern-candidate-grafting]]: the plan-arbiter *Hybrid* outcome and its *Borrowed From Other Plans* section ([[builder-plan-arbiter]]). - [[pattern-source-grounding]]: **signature** of [[builder-read-the-damn-docs]]; official docs over model memory. - [[pattern-idempotent-operations]]: recovery that never repeats a completed write, reply, approval, merge, or deploy ([[builder-factory-recover]]). - [[pattern-session-handoff]]: self-contained wake prompts and blocked-state handoffs ([[builder-stay-within-limits]], [[builder-factory-recover]], [[builder-plow-ahead]]). - [[pattern-systematic-debugging]]: recurrence traced to a shared boundary, confirmed causes separated from hypotheses, and a stated test that would disprove each ([[builder-factory-lookback]]). - [[pattern-knowledge-compounding]]: a proven workflow packaged into a reusable app ([[builder-turn-into-app]]); production recurrence folded into systemic fixes ([[builder-factory-lookback]]). - [[pattern-fresh-context-subagents]]: handoff packets written *"as if the subagent has no useful chat context"* ([[builder-efficient-fable]], [[builder-efficient-frontier]]). - [[pattern-wave-parallelism]]: bounded waves of at most three parallel subagents, with a usage check between waves ([[builder-stay-within-limits]]). ## See Also - [[topic-software-factory]]: where the Factory fills the empty prompt-owned control-plane cell of the design grid. [[sssf]] is the direct opposite bet (control plane in code). [[gh-aw]] is the nearest runtime relative, with standing repository automation behind gated write channels, but it compiles the gates into CI where the Factory writes them as prose policy. - [[pstack]]: the other framework with a report-triggered, low-authority automation pack. [[pstack-benny-triage]] ↔ [[builder-factory-collect]]; [[pstack-principle-never-block-on-the-human]] ↔ [[builder-plow-ahead]]; [[pstack-show-me-your-work]] ↔ the plow-ahead decision recap. pstack's Cursor built-in `/babysit` is the same idea as [[builder-factory-babysit-pr]]. - [[compound-engineering]]: [[ce-resolve-pr-feedback]] ↔ [[builder-factory-babysit-pr]]; [[ce-sweep]] ↔ [[builder-factory-collect]]; [[ce-product-pulse]] is the nearest earlier production-signal report. - [[addy-agent-skills]]: [[addy-source-driven-development]] ↔ [[builder-read-the-damn-docs]]. - [[beads]]: `bd human` is the store-layer counterpart of [[builder-factory-human-digest]]. - [[stage-align]] · [[stage-plan]] · [[stage-implement]] · [[stage-review]] · [[stage-release]] · [[stage-learn]]: the six stages these capabilities feed. There is **no [[stage-specify]]** and **no [[stage-validate]]** capability. Validation is folded into ship and collect as *"run the configured checks"*.

# /ce-sweep

`/ce-sweep` — "Ingest Slack/GitHub items since cursors, acknowledge at source, analyze, verify fixes, reconcile plans." A lifecycle-tracking / feedback-consolidation skill: it pulls new items (Slack messages, GitHub issues/PRs) since the last cursor, acknowledges them at the source, analyzes and de-duplicates them, verifies whether reported issues are already fixed, and reconciles the findings back into existing plans.

It is a **feedback-intake** capability at the front of the loop — turning external signal into actionable inputs for the next [[ce-brainstorm]]/[[ce-plan]] cycle — so it implements [[stage-align]]. It has a foot in [[stage-learn]] too (consolidating what was learned from shipped work), but its primary act is *intake that seeds the next iteration*. No direct cross-framework counterpart; conceptually adjacent to [[ce-product-pulse]] (which reports post-release signal) and to the compound loop's grounding reads.

## See Also
- [[ce-product-pulse]] — post-release reporting sibling; `ce-sweep` turns signal into plan inputs.
- `ce-riffrec-feedback-analysis` — structures a specific feedback source (catalogued on [[compound-engineering]], not separately paged).
- [[stage-align]] — the canonical stage this implements.

"""Audit another agent's work, given a Codex session ID, a Claude Code transcript, a PR, a branch, a CI run, or a pasted summary. **The idea worth taking: investigate independently, then diff.** *"Anchoring is the failure mode: reading their work first and nodding along."* The watchdog forms its own hypotheses, ideally before reading the other agent's conclusions, and uses the wait while that agent is still running to pre-map the problem. It prioritizes evidence the watched agent probably did not look at: production ledgers, session replays, error trackers, deploy state, and other worktrees. It then diffs the two investigations (what each found that the other missed, where the approaches diverge, and *"any product or design fork they took silently"*) and turns the difference into concrete add-on directions to pass along.

"""Turn competing plans from several agents (*"such as Codex and Claude Code"*) into **one executable direction**. It aims to *"produce a clear handoff instead of a blended mush."*

+# /agent-watchdog

+Audit another agent's work, given a Codex session ID, a Claude Code transcript, a PR, a branch, a CI run, or a pasted summary. The skill describes itself as *"a reviewer with a pager who is also a second investigator."* It has four modes, inferred from the request: watch only, audit, audit and fix, and compare. *"If authority is unclear, default to audit-only."*

+**The idea worth taking: investigate independently, then diff.** *"Anchoring is the failure mode: reading their work first and nodding along."* The watchdog forms its own hypotheses, ideally before reading the other agent's conclusions, and uses the wait while that agent is still running to pre-map the problem. It prioritizes evidence the watched agent probably did not look at: production ledgers, session replays, error trackers, deploy state, and other worktrees. It then diffs the two investigations (what each found that the other missed, where the approaches diverge, and *"any product or design fork they took silently"*) and turns the difference into concrete add-on directions to pass along.

+**Relay sparingly.** A mid-run agent *"re-plans around every note it receives"*, so the watchdog interrupts only for a defect in code being touched now, a correction, or an answer the agent is blocked on. Everything else waits for a checkpoint and goes as one batch. *"Never hand a mid-run agent an unranked list… an unranked backlog reliably produces several half-finished surfaces instead of a few complete ones."* It also reports what it verified as correct, *"so they stop re-litigating settled ground."*

+It classifies each issue as a gap, a bug, a verification miss, scope drift, or no issue. [[stage-review]], with the reviewer set up as a separate agent (often a different vendor) instead of a subagent of the author: [[pattern-cross-model-review]] at the level of whole sessions.

Reads `.agent-factory/config.yaml` ([[artifact-autonomy-policy]]) and its own optional `skill_prompts` overlay, which adds project guidance but cannot grant permission. It follows **one explicitly authorized PR** through its delivery lifecycle. *"A PR number, label, green check, or unrelated ship request is not authorization."*

+Each pass has five steps. (1) **Confirm authority and ownership**: exact host, repository, PR, the original user authorization, allowed paths and risk, and a task-owned worktree, stopping before any write if something is missing or stale. (2) **Read a complete live snapshot**: base and head, open/draft/merged state, all required checks, reviews, unresolved threads, and mergeability. *"Partial or unavailable data is unknown, not clean."* (3) **Disposition feedback**: fix only actionable findings within the authorized limits, and *"avoid speculative cleanup and larger redesigns."* (4) **Verify and re-read**: after every push, fetch the live PR again and tie all evidence to the new head. (5) **Apply action gates separately.**

+The action-gate table has six rows: Fix, Publish (*"never force-push or overwrite a concurrent update"*), Reply, Approve, Merge (*only if the host can condition the merge on the checked head*), and **Soak**. For the soak, the agent must *"prove the exact head and required gates stayed unchanged for the full configured interval. # Artifact: Decision log

A **single append-only TSV, one row per decision**, kept while an agent works unattended so a human who stepped away can audit what happened and decide whether to trust the result.

Six columns: `ts` (ISO8601), `phase`, `decision` (what was chosen, one line), `why` (the reason in plain words, *not* a jargon tag), `evidence` (a commit SHA, PR number, `file:line`, or an artifact, trace, or screenshot path — **never a paragraph**), and `result` (the outcome or predicate state: `tests green`, `reverted`, `pixel-diff 0`, `INCONCLUSIVE`, `open`).

```
ts	phase	decision	why	evidence	result
2026-05-24T09:40:00Z	harness	took screenshots of the old version before changing anything	so we can compare old against new and catch any visual change	scripts/snapshot.sh, baseline/	saved 120 reference screenshots
2026-05-24T11:15:00Z	widget	moved the widget styles over without changing how it looks	keep the change small and the result identical	commit 7c21e0a, pixel-diff 0	looks identical, tests pass
2026-05-24T12:30:00Z	widget	threw out a helper's work because its screenshots were blank	checked the real files instead of trusting its summary	worktree reset	reverted, tightened the instructions for next time
```

**Its distinguishing property among this wiki's artifacts is its reader.** [[artifact-handoff-doc]] and the state a work [[beads|store]] holds exist so the *next agent* can continue; a retrospective ([[artifact-retrospective]]) and a solution corpus ([[artifact-solution-doc]]) exist so *future work* starts ahead. A decision log exists so a **human who was not watching can reconstruct the reasoning after the fact** and locate the point where trust should stop. That is why evidence is a pointer rather than prose, why rows are single-line, and why the third example row above is a *reverted* decision — the log's value is concentrated in the moments the run went wrong.

Three rules govern it. **Append-only**: a wrong call gets a new row that supersedes it; history is never edited or deleted. **Decision points and checkpoints only** — a fork chosen, a unit completed with its verification result, a pivot or revert with its trigger, a blocker surfaced, a gate fixed — not every action. And **prefer evidence produced by committed scripts** over hand-made one-offs ([[pattern-tooling-leverage]]).

**Where it lives is a deliberate default.** It is a working artifact at `decisions.tsv` (or `.audit/<task-slug>.tsv` when several efforts run at once) and is left out of git, committed only when the work is ambitious enough that a reviewer needs the trail to trust the result. The trail is always kept; it becomes a repository artifact only when it has a reader.

# Pattern: Action gating (authority decomposed per external action)

Split an agent's authority into **separately authorized kinds of external action** (fix, publish, reply, review, approve, merge, deploy, close, recover, notify). Give each its own policy, **never infer permission for one from another**, and recheck live state right before each write. Permission to fix a bug does not include replying to the reporter, and approving a PR does not include merging it. A merge does not include deploying.

The Factory in [[builder-skills]] states the rule most compactly: *"Fix, reply, close, review, approve, publish, merge, deploy, recover, and notify are independent decisions."* Its [[artifact-autonomy-policy]] gives each action a policy of `never`, `manual`, `criteria` (explicit `allow` and `stop` lists, where *all* allow conditions must pass and *no* stop condition may apply), or a named proof point (`after-fix`, `after-merge`). The default for anything unclear is to hold: *"Missing, unclear, or unavailable evidence means hold."*

**How it differs from its neighbours.** [[pattern-edit-guardrails]] limits what the agent may *write or touch* inside the workspace. [[pattern-deterministic-gates]] decides whether the *work* is good enough to accept. Action gating decides which of the agent's **effects on the outside world** it is allowed to cause, and it decides each one separately. The pattern exists because unattended agents fail at the boundary between steps. An agent allowed to fix and ship will, left alone, treat a green fix as permission to merge. Splitting authority at every external write is the fix, and in the Factory it goes as far as the notification layer (`DONT_NOTIFY` when nothing verifiable changed).

**Three details make it work in practice.**

- **Authorization is re-established, never assumed.** A PR number, label, green check, task title, or agent summary *"is not authorization"*. The original user request is re-read on every pass.
- **Evidence expires with the head.** Approval and merge evidence is tied to one exact head revision, and *"a changed head invalidates old check/review evidence and resets the soak."* A merge is conditioned on that head when the host supports it. When the host does not, the dependent action stays disabled.
- **Prompt text cannot widen it.** Project overlays add guidance but *"cannot grant permission, or weaken repository and host safeguards"*. On conflict, the more restrictive rule wins.

## Applied by (backlinks)

builder-skills (the signature instance):

- [[builder-factory]] sets the ten independent policies and their safe defaults. Replies, closure, approvals, merges, deploys, and recovery are off unless explicitly enabled.
- [[builder-factory-babysit-pr]] has a six-row gate table (Fix, Publish, Reply, Approve, Merge, Soak) for one authorized PR.
- [[builder-factory-review-prs]] keeps review findings separate from reply, approval, and merge.
- [[builder-factory-ship]] treats merge and deploy verification as separate proof points: *"a merge is not live proof."*
- [[builder-factory-collect]] and [[builder-factory-lookback]] only investigate when they find a problem or a recurring pattern. Replying, closing, and fixing each need their own authorization.
- [[builder-factory-human-digest]] is read-only by construction and routes every decision back to the module that owns it.
- [[builder-factory-watchdog]] and [[builder-factory-recover]] notify only on a verified next step and never repeat a completed write.

pstack (the earlier instance, stated as *autonomy decoupled from authority*):

- [[pstack-benny-reproduce-and-fix]] runs fully unattended and still stops at a **bounded draft PR**, with no merge authority at all.

## Enabled by (infrastructure)

- [[gh-aw]]: **safe outputs** are the structural form of this pattern. The agent job has no write permission. Each kind of write (create-issue, add-comment, create-pull-request, …) is a separate typed output applied by a separate job with a minimally scoped token, after a threat-detection verdict. The Factory writes its gates as prose policy the agent must follow. gh-aw compiles them into the CI job graph, where the agent cannot break them.

## See Also
- [[pattern-edit-guardrails]]: the neighbour that limits workspace writes rather than external actions.
- [[pattern-deterministic-gates]]: the gates that decide whether work is acceptable. Action gating decides what may be *done* with it.
- [[pattern-evidence-before-claims]]: the rule underneath every gate here. Unavailable is not empty, and a label is not proof.
- [[pattern-autonomous-loop]]: the pattern this makes safe to run unattended.
